passages.original: Mon. 41, 34 θοόϲ: τὰ εἰϲ οϲ καθαρὰ διϲύλλαβα τῷ ο παραληγόμενα φιλεῖ βαρύνεϲθαι κόοϲ, ϲόοϲ, νόοϲ, χνόοϲ, γόοϲ, πλόοϲ, ῥόοϲ, θρόοϲ. διὸ καὶ τὸ ζόοϲ παῤ Ἐπιχάρμῳ οἱ πλείουϲ ἐβάρυναν «τρὶϲ ἀπεδόθη ζόοϲ» ὁμοίωϲ καὶ τὸ ϲόοϲ. τὸ μέντοι θοόϲ ἄντικρυϲ ὀξυνόμενον μονῆρεϲ. τὰ δὲ αἴτια τούτων ἐν ἑτέροιϲ δηλοῦμεν.
passages.english: Mon. 41, 34: *thoos* ("swift"): disyllables ending in *-os* that are pure (with a vowel before the ending) and have *o* in the penultimate syllable are usually barytone (unaccented on the final syllable): *koos*, *soos*, *noos*, *chnoos*, *goos*, *ploos*, *rhoos*, *throos*. For this reason most [grammarians] also made *zoos* in Epicharmus barytone, "*zoos* was given back three times", and likewise *soos*. *Thoos*, however, being oxytone (accented on the final syllable) in direct opposition [to this rule], is unique. The reasons for these things we set out elsewhere.
passages.notes: "Mon. 41, 34" is a reference to Herodian's Περὶ μονήρους λέξεως (On Unique Words), as printed in the edition. The Greek words are given in transliteration because the point is their accentuation. In "pure" (καθαρά) disyllables a vowel precedes the ending. The Epicharmus fragment «τρὶϲ ἀπεδόθη ζόοϲ» is short and without context, so its sense is uncertain. ζόοϲ apparently means "life" (a form of ζωός/ζωή), and the line may mean "life was restored three times".
